"Fifty-two in maths." Parveen dropped the report card on the kitchen table. "And Abbu's shop is shut since March. Great year."
Sarita, from the flat upstairs, stopped peeling peas. "Fifty-two isn't zero."
"It's not ninety either. Ammi was counting on me."
"Did she say that?"
"No. She said, 'Eat something.' That's worse."
"What went wrong in the paper?"
"Geometry. I left the whole section."
"So it's one section, not your whole brain."
Parveen almost smiled. "You sound like a poster, Didi."
"I failed chemistry in Class 11," Sarita said. "Cried in the lift. Then I did old papers every Sunday with Anil Bhaiya. Passed with seventy."
"You never told me."
"You never failed before." Sarita pushed the bowl across. "Peel. Then we list the geometry chapters. Two a week."
Parveen took a pod, and after a moment, a pencil.

passage: I'm Samir, and the winter my parents stopped talking to each other, I stopped doing homework. Papa slept on the sofa. Mummy spoke to him through me: "Tell your father the gas bill came." My half-yearly card came back with two reds. I hid it in my cricket bag for a week. It was Uday who found it, looking for his gloves. He didn't lecture. He said, "My parents did this in Class 7. It's not about you, but it lands on you." That sentence stuck. I asked my class teacher if I could do homework in the library after school, where it was quiet. I told Mummy the message-carrying had to stop. She cried, then agreed. Home isn't fixed. But my maths is back to a pass, and I don't dread the walk home every evening.

qa.a: In the cricket bag.

qa.a: A quiet library space and asking Mummy to stop sending messages through Samir both helped; a counsellor could offer a regular place to talk while home stays unsettled.

qa.a: Uday recognises it from his own Class 7, so he sees Samir not as lazy but as someone caught in the parents' conflict.

The monsoon failed in the village that year. Ojas's father's cotton crop dried up in the field. At night, Ojas heard his parents arguing about the loan.
He stopped going to cricket. He sat by the dry well with his books but didn't read.
His friend Irfan found him there. "My Abba says the whole village is struggling. The sarpanch is calling a meeting about the crop relief scheme."

Ojas nodded. He went to cricket the next day.

In Osaka, the results for the high school entrance exam were posted online at 10 a.m. Aiko's number wasn't there. She checked three times.
She didn't cry until she reached the river path, where Kwame, her friend from the running club, found her.
"I studied every day for a year," she said. "My mother told everyone."
Kwame sat down. "My brother failed his first one too. He went to his second-choice school, and now he's at university."
"That's different."
"Maybe. But one exam isn't your whole life."
Aiko went home. Her mother hugged her before she said anything. That evening they looked at the second-choice school's brochure together. It had a strong science club. Aiko didn't feel happy. But for the first time that day, she felt something like hope.

qa.a: At 10 a.m.

qa.a: Aiko felt crushed and disappointed, and worried about letting her mother down after a year of studying.

qa.q: What helped Aiko begin to cope, and why?
qa.a: Kwame's story about a brother and her mother's hug without blame helped, and looking at a real next option gave her something to move toward.

qa.q: What was it like for Aiko's mother to see her daughter come home?
qa.a: Her mother was probably sad for Aiko but wanted her to feel loved first, which is why she hugged her before she said anything.

In the school counsellor's room, Hafsa sat with her hands tucked under her legs. Her father's shop had closed last month. She'd quietly dropped out of the school trip and stopped going to tuition, and she'd been walking her little brother Farhan home early to cook, because her mother was working longer shifts.
"I don't want anyone to know," she said. "Everyone will pity us."
The counsellor didn't push. She asked what Hafsa was worried about most. "Falling behind. And Farhan. He cries at night."
They made a plan: the school had a free study group after classes that Hafsa could join, and the counsellor would talk to Farhan's teacher, privately. She also asked if she could call Hafsa's mother. Hafsa nodded.
Walking out, Hafsa still felt heavy. But lighter than when she'd come in.

qa.a: Hafsa felt ashamed and afraid of being pitied by others.

qa.a: She asked what worried Hafsa most, offered a free study group and private support for Farhan, and asked permission before calling her mother.

She said she'd call Amma, and she did, that same evening. I made a timetable with just those three chapters. Some nights I cried first and studied after. The boards are in March. I'm not okay every day, but I'm not giving up either.
